title: "4.2.3 Emergent Time"

Suppose time is not fundamental. Suppose what we call time is a feature that emerges from a deeper, timeless level of reality: the way temperature emerges from molecular motion, or the way solidity emerges from atomic lattices. The fundamental description of the world, on this proposal, makes no reference to time; time is a useful approximation at our scale, a coarse-grained feature that drops out of the deeper physics in the appropriate limit. If this is right, then the structural account of §2.6 is at best a description of the emergent layer, not of fundamental reality. The classical theist, sensing again an opening, can locate the changeless ground at the timeless fundamental level and the structural roles at the emergent surface.

The move is not idle. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation, the canonical equation of quantum gravity, contains no time variable; the wavefunction of the universe is timeless, and the appearance of time in our experience is to be recovered (somehow) from a fundamentally timeless formalism. @pageWootters1983 develop the most influential proposal: time emerges as a correlation between subsystems of a timeless universe, with one subsystem serving as a clock for the rest. Barbour's *The End of Time* [-@barbour1999] develops Platonia: a timeless configuration space from which temporal experience emerges as “time capsules,” configurations that happen to encode apparent memories. Rovelli's *The Order of Time* [-@rovelli2018] offers a relational account: time is the structure of correlations between physical systems, not a fundamental backdrop. Smolin's *Time Reborn* [-@smolin2013] takes the opposite line, defending time's fundamentality, but the position the present reply targets is the timeless-fundamental position, not Smolin's.

In the philosophy of time, kindred views include Albert's *Time and Chance* [-@albert2000], which derives temporal asymmetry from the past-hypothesis and statistical-mechanical considerations; Price's *Time's Arrow and Archimedes' Point* [-@price1996], which argues that the apparent directedness of time is a perspectival feature; Reichenbach's *The Direction of Time* [-@reichenbach1956], the classical mid-century treatment of time's arrow; Maudlin's *The Metaphysics Within Physics* [-@maudlin2007], which defends time's fundamentality against eliminativist readings. Anderson's *The Problem of Time* [-@andersonEdward2017] gives the technical state of play in canonical quantum gravity. The literature is vast and the technical questions are subtle. The present reply targets the structural claim: that time is derivative rather than fundamental, and therefore that the structural conditions of §2.6 obtain at most at an emergent layer.

Three forms of the move develop the position at three depths: the strict-emergence form, the correlational-time form, and the relational-time form. The reply argues that each fails for the same structural reason at increasing levels of refinement.

*First.* The strict-emergence form claims that the fundamental level is timeless and that time is a phenomenon of the emergent layer only, in the way that temperature is a phenomenon of bulk thermodynamics and not of individual molecules. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation, on this reading, describes a fundamentally timeless universe, and the appearance of time at our scale is a coarse-grained illusion.

The analogy with temperature does not carry the weight the position needs. Temperature is emergent in the sense that it is a statistical property of an underlying dynamics that is itself temporal: the molecules move, collide, and exchange energy in time, and the bulk property of temperature is a statistical summary of that temporal dynamics. The molecular dynamics is not itself temperature, but it is itself temporal; the emergence is from a more fundamental temporal description to a less fundamental temporal description. For time itself to be emergent in the analogous sense would require a more fundamental description that is itself non-temporal but supports the emergence of time, and this is exactly what the strict-emergence form needs and exactly what the position cannot supply. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation does not describe a non-temporal dynamics from which time emerges; it describes a wavefunction satisfying a constraint, and the recovery of time from the wavefunction is the open problem the field has been working on for decades. To call the formalism “timeless” is to describe the constraint, not the dynamics; the dynamics, if there is to be one, is what the recovery program is meant to produce.

The deeper structural point: any proposed fundamental level that supports the emergence of time must contain the resources for time to emerge from it. Those resources are the structural roles §2.6 names. Distinctness of fundamental states (S), an ordering across them sufficient to support the emergent direction (T), and a persistence spanning the ordering sufficient to underwrite the emergent identity of objects across the emergent time (Φ). The fundamental level can be called “timeless” only in the restricted sense that it does not contain time as we recognize time at our scale. It cannot be timeless in the sense of lacking the structural roles: if it lacked them, no time could emerge from it.

*Second.* The Page–Wootters correlational form is more refined: time emerges as the correlation between two subsystems of a timeless universe, with one subsystem (the clock) serving as a reference relative to which the other subsystem (the rest) appears to evolve. Mathematically, the global wavefunction is timeless; the conditional wavefunction (conditioning on the clock state) evolves in the clock variable. The conditional evolution is what we observe as time.

The correlation between subsystems requires distinctness of subsystems (S), an ordering of clock states sufficient to support the conditional evolution (T), and a persistence of the universal wavefunction across the conditional structure (Φ). The Page–Wootters construction is internally coherent and structurally informative: it shows that something that looks like time at one level can be derived from a timeless-looking formalism at another level. What it does not show is that the structural roles are absent at the fundamental level. The clock subsystem must be distinct from the rest (S obtains). The clock states must stand in an ordering that the conditional evolution tracks (T obtains in the clock structure). The universal wavefunction must persist across the conditional construction (Φ obtains globally). The construction is a relabeling of where T is located (in the clock variable rather than in a global parameter), not an elimination of T.

*Third.* The relational-time form, developed most influentially by Rovelli, claims that time is not a backdrop in which physical systems evolve but a structure of correlations between physical systems. There is no absolute time; there is only the relative evolution of one system with respect to another. Each system is a clock for the others, and the appearance of a universal time is the coarse-grained agreement of many such relative clocks.

Relational time is a thesis about the metaphysics of time, not its elimination. Rovelli's view is closer to Leibnizian relationism than to eliminativism: time consists in relations between physical systems rather than in an absolute backdrop, but the relations are real and structural and do the work that absolute time was supposed to do. The reply, accordingly, is not that relationism is incoherent (it is not) but that relationism is not a refutation of the structural conditions: it is a relocation of where the conditions are instantiated. The relations are between distinct systems (S), they support directed evolution (T), and they persist across the systems' interactions (Φ). Relational time *is* the structural conditions of §2.6 in a relationist metaphysics.

A kindred move is the past-hypothesis style derivation (Albert, Price): the apparent directedness of time is derived from a low-entropy initial condition plus statistical mechanics, with no fundamental time-asymmetric law. The reply is the same. The derivation requires distinctness of microstates (S), an ordering across them sufficient to define entropy increase (T), and a dynamical evolution that preserves the relevant structural facts across the increase (Φ). The asymmetry of time is derived from the past-hypothesis, but the symmetric temporal structure is presupposed by the derivation, not eliminated by it.

Another kindred is the eternalist/B-theoretic position that the appearance of temporal becoming is a perspectival feature of conscious experience while the world itself is a four-dimensional manifold without genuine becoming. This is treated separately at §4.2.6 (the B-theoretic block). The B-theoretic eternalist accepts T (the four-dimensional manifold is temporally extended) and contests only the metaphysical reality of A-series becoming. The dispute is therefore not about whether T obtains but about its metaphysical character.

*What converges.* Three forms and none lets the elimination of T at the fundamental level stand. Strict emergence cannot supply a non-temporal fundamental dynamics; the Wheeler–DeWitt ‘timelessness’ is a constraint on the wavefunction, not a non-temporal dynamics from which time can emerge. The Page–Wootters construction relocates T from a global parameter to a clock subsystem; relocation is not elimination. Relational time is a metaphysics of time as relations between systems, not an elimination of the structural role time plays. Each move produces a redescription of where the structural conditions are located, not a description of a world in which they are absent. The shared failure is structural: *timeless* and *never* are parasitic negations of Time, quantifiers internal to the temporal domain rather than substrates outside it (§2.1.5, Parasitic Negation). A ¬∃t (the assertion that there is no t, no temporal coordinate, no instant) cannot ground an emergence of time, since a quantifier is not a level. The three forms collapse into relocations because there is nothing else coherent for them to be.

Sibling counter-constructions: the changeless-ground objection, on which a timeless being grounds the structure from outside, is §4.2.1. The Shoemaker objection, on which time can obtain without change, is §4.2.2. The momentariness objection, on which persistence is illusory, is §4.2.8. The B-theoretic block objection, on which the temporal manifold lacks genuine becoming, is §4.2.6.

What the emergent-time literature genuinely establishes is worth preserving: the time of our experience is not the time of fundamental physics in any direct mapping. The clock-based time of relativity is not the conditional time of canonical quantum gravity; the entropic arrow is not the relativistic light-cone structure; the phenomenal flow of conscious experience is not the parameter of the Schrödinger equation. There are many time-like structures in physics, and the relations between them are subtle and partially open. The structural account of §2.6 is consistent with this plurality. What the account requires is that any proposed fundamental level that supports the emergence or relocation or relabeling of time-like structure contains the resources (distinctness, ordering, persistence) for that emergence or relocation or relabeling to be possible. The structural roles are not the time of any particular physical theory; they are the conditions any theory must instantiate to have time-like structure at all.

The research program around the Wheeler–DeWitt equation has occupied physicists for over half a century; no consensus on the recovery of time has emerged. What has emerged is a more careful articulation of what the structural conditions of time actually are, and the present reply is a beneficiary of that articulation. The fundamental level may turn out to be very different from the time of our experience. It will not turn out to be without distinctness, ordering, and persistence, because if it were, no time could emerge from it, and the recovery program would have nothing to recover.
